options.text: Tapering prevents symptoms from returning in the long term, which is why NICE always recommends it for every woman.
options.why: NICE indicates that gradual reduction makes no difference in the long term and offers a choice between both.

options.text: She must stop abruptly, because NICE considers that tapering prolongs symptoms.
options.why: NICE does not impose abrupt stopping: it offers a choice, and tapering may limit short-term recurrence.

options.text: She can choose: tapering may limit short-term recurrence, but makes no long-term difference.
options.why: Correct: this is what NICE asks clinicians to explain; it can also be restarted if needed.

options.text: Once stopped, NICE advises against starting HRT again even if the same symptoms return.
options.why: NICE explains that symptoms may return and that HRT can be restarted if needed.

items.explanation: NICE recommends offering a choice between gradual reduction and stopping immediately: gradual reduction may limit symptom recurrence in the short term, but makes no difference in the longer term. Symptoms may return and HRT can be restarted.

items.stem: According to NAMS 2022, in which situation could a compounded hormone preparation be considered?

options.text: When the patient prefers it because she considers it more natural than approved products.
options.why: NAMS states that patient preference alone does not justify its use (Level III).

options.text: When a saliva test shows a deficit of several hormones that need combining.
options.why: NAMS considers saliva testing unreliable and does not recommend it for dosing.

options.text: When a sustained-release route such as pellets is wanted, to avoid daily dosing.
options.why: Pellets are among the untested routes NAMS mentions when describing compounded preparations.

options.text: When an approved product cannot be used, because of allergy to an ingredient or the needed dose is unavailable.
options.why: Correct: these are the examples NAMS gives (Level III).

items.explanation: NAMS discourages compounded preparations because of minimal regulation, overdosing and underdosing, impurities, lack of sterility and data, and no label. It considers them only when an approved product cannot be used, for example because of allergy to an ingredient or because the needed dose or formulation is unavailable.

items.stem: A patient with a uterus wants “bioidentical” estradiol and progesterone together in a single capsule, but authorised. Which option authorised in Spain meets her request?

options.text: Bijuva, which combines estradiol 1 mg and progesterone 100 mg.
options.why: Correct: it is a product authorised in Spain that combines both hormones.

options.text: Progeffik 200 mg, which combines micronized progesterone and estradiol in one capsule.
options.why: Progeffik is micronized progesterone alone (100 and 200 mg), authorised as an adjunct to estrogen.

options.text: A compounded troche with estriol, DHEA and testosterone.
options.why: This is exactly the type of untested compounded combination NAMS discourages; it is not an authorised product.

options.text: Utrogestan, which combines both hormones in a single capsule.
options.why: Utrogestan is micronized progesterone alone, with no estradiol: in Spain it is marketed as 200, 300 and 400 mg vaginal capsules, and the cited source also places it in ANMAT’s formulary in Argentina (100 and 200 mg).

items.explanation: If the goal is a hormone “identical to her own” with quality control, authorised options exist: in Spain, Progeffik (micronized progesterone 100 and 200 mg) and Bijuva (estradiol 1 mg and progesterone 100 mg); in Argentina, ANMAT’s formulary includes Utrogestan (100 and 200 mg).

items.stem: According to NICE NG23, what did menopause-specific cognitive behavioural therapy mainly improve for VMS?

options.text: Only hot flash frequency, with no change in their severity or in how bothersome they were.
options.why: NICE describes improvements in frequency and severity and, above all, in how bothersome they were.

options.text: Bone mineral density and fracture risk, in addition to VMS.
options.why: NICE does not attribute bone effects to CBT; NAMS describes that for hormone therapy.

options.text: Above all how bothersome the symptoms were, as well as their frequency and severity.
options.why: Correct: this is how NICE summarises it, with design limitations and potential bias in the evidence.

options.text: Nothing measurable: NICE concluded the evidence showed no effect on VMS.
options.why: NICE recommends considering it precisely because it observed improvements, albeit with evidence limitations.

items.explanation: NICE recommends considering menopause-specific CBT as an option for VMS, alongside HRT, when HRT is contraindicated or not preferred. Its rationale describes improvements in frequency, severity and, above all, in how bothersome symptoms were, with design limitations and potential bias.

items.stem: A patient who does not want HRT asks about clinical hypnosis for her hot flashes. Which best reflects what the sources say?

options.text: NAMS recommends it at Level I; NICE NG23 does not address hypnosis, but does recommend considering CBT.
options.why: Correct: NICE not addressing it is not the same as advising against it.

options.text: NAMS recommends it at Level I; NICE NG23 expressly advises against it for lack of evidence.
options.why: NICE NG23 does not address hypnosis: it neither recommends nor advises against it.

options.text: Neither source recommends it, like paced respiration and mindfulness.
options.why: NAMS does recommend clinical hypnosis (Level I); paced respiration and mindfulness are what it does not recommend.

options.text: Both recommend it as first line ahead of HRT, at Level I.
options.why: NICE does not address hypnosis and assigns no levels; NAMS does not place it ahead of HRT.

items.explanation: NAMS 2023 recommends CBT and clinical hypnosis (Level I); in one trial, hypnosis reduced hot flash frequency by 74% versus 17% with an attention control. NICE NG23 recommends considering menopause-specific CBT but does not address hypnosis.

items.stem: Which of these doses matches the NAMS 2023 table of non-hormonal drugs for VMS?

options.text: Gabapentin, 100–300 mg/day as a single bedtime dose.
options.why: Invented dose: the table gives 900–2,400 mg/day in divided doses.

options.text: Venlafaxine, 300–450 mg/day in divided doses.
options.why: Invented dose: the table gives 37.5–150 mg/day.

options.text: Paroxetine, 40–60 mg/day as a single dose.
options.why: Invented dose: the table gives 7.5 mg/day (FDA-approved salt) or 10–25 mg/day.

options.text: Fezolinetant, 45 mg/day as a single dose.
options.why: Correct: this is the dose in the NAMS table.

items.explanation: Doses from the NAMS 2023 table: paroxetine salt 7.5 mg/day (FDA approved for VMS); paroxetine 10–25 mg/day; citalopram and escitalopram 10–20 mg/day; venlafaxine 37.5–150 mg/day; desvenlafaxine 100–150 mg/day; gabapentin 900–2,400 mg/day in divided doses; fezolinetant 45 mg/day.

items.stem: On SSRIs/SNRIs for VMS, which sentence reflects the difference between NAMS 2023 and NICE NG23?

options.text: NAMS recommends them (Level I); NICE advises against routinely offering them first line for VMS alone.
options.why: Correct: this is a real disagreement; NICE’s wording dates from 2015.

options.text: Both recommend them as first line for VMS, ahead of fezolinetant.
options.why: NICE advises against routinely offering them as first line for VMS alone.

options.text: NAMS does not recommend them for lack of efficacy; NICE proposes them when HRT is unsuitable.
options.why: NAMS does recommend them (Level I); what NICE proposes when HRT is unsuitable is fezolinetant.

options.text: Both advise against them equally, along with clonidine, for any patient with VMS.
options.why: NAMS recommends them; they only coincide on clonidine, which NAMS does not recommend and NICE does not routinely offer first line.

items.explanation: For NAMS 2023, SSRIs/SNRIs, gabapentin and fezolinetant are Level I options. NICE, with 2015 wording, advises against routinely offering SSRIs, SNRIs or clonidine first line for VMS alone, and recommends fezolinetant as an option for moderate to severe VMS when HRT is unsuitable.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman (fictional case) who cannot take HRT mainly has night sweats that wake her up. If gabapentin is chosen, what does NAMS 2023 suggest?

options.text: Take it in the morning, because it causes insomnia and would worsen sleep if taken at night.
options.why: It is the other way round: drowsiness is an adverse effect, which is why NAMS suggests bedtime dosing.

options.text: Avoid it, because NAMS does not recommend it for VMS given its adverse-effect profile.
options.why: NAMS does recommend gabapentin (Level I); the one it does not recommend is pregabalin.

options.text: Always combine it with oxybutynin to boost the effect on night sweats.
options.why: NAMS does not propose that combination, and warns of possible cognitive decline with long-term oxybutynin in older people.

options.text: Bedtime dosing, because it initially causes drowsiness and dizziness and her night-time VMS disrupt sleep.
options.why: Correct: this is NAMS’s suggestion for women whose sleep is disrupted by VMS.

items.explanation: Gabapentin (900–2,400 mg/day in divided doses) is a Level I option for NAMS. As it initially causes dizziness and drowsiness, bedtime dosing may suit women whose night-time VMS disrupt sleep.

items.stem: A 56-year-old woman (fictional case) in Spain is about to start fezolinetant (Veoza). Her baseline ALT is 2.5 times the upper limit of normal. According to the EU product information, which is correct?

options.text: Do not start it: with ALT or AST ≥ 2 times the upper limit it should not be initiated.
options.why: Correct: this is the threshold the product information sets for not starting treatment.

options.text: Start and repeat ALT at 6 and 9 months, which is the EU product information schedule.
options.why: Checks at 6 and 9 months are those added by the FDA label; moreover, with ALT ≥ 2 times the limit it should not be started.

options.text: Start it without further checks: liver enzyme elevation was rare in the trials.
options.why: Its rarity in trials does not exempt from the checks the product information requires.

options.text: Start it at half dose and check ALT only if liver symptoms appear.
options.why: The product information does not propose half dose, and requires monthly liver tests for the first 3 months.

items.explanation: The Veoza product information in Spain and the EU requires liver tests before starting, monthly for the first 3 months and then as clinically indicated, and not starting if ALT or AST is ≥ 2 times the upper limit or total bilirubin is elevated. The FDA label adds a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity and checks at 6 and 9 months.

items.stem: According to NAMS 2023, how are soy, soy extracts and equol classified for VMS?

options.text: Not recommended (Level II), because of mixed evidence from small, heterogeneous and short studies.
options.why: Correct: this is how NAMS 2023 classifies them.

options.text: Recommended (Level I), because all women convert daidzein to equol.
options.why: They are not recommended, and only 35% of North American women metabolise daidzein to equol.

options.text: Recommended (Level II) only in women who metabolise daidzein to equol.
options.why: NAMS does not recommend them in any subgroup; equol metabolism is cited as a limitation.

options.text: Not recommended (Level I), because of hepatotoxicity proven in large trials.
options.why: The reason is mixed evidence (Level II); the liver warning concerns black cohosh.

items.explanation: NAMS 2023 does not recommend soy, soy extracts or equol (Level II): the studies are small, heterogeneous and short, and only 35% of North American women metabolise daidzein to equol.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman (fictional case) on tamoxifen is taking St John’s wort on her own for hot flashes. According to NICE NG23, what do you explain?

options.text: That NICE recommends it for women with breast cancer because it does not interact with tamoxifen.
options.why: NICE specifically warns of serious interactions, for example with tamoxifen.

options.text: That NICE considers it ineffective and harmless, so she can simply keep taking it.
options.why: NICE accepts it may relieve VMS, but warns of serious interactions and uncertainties.

options.text: That it may relieve VMS, but there is uncertainty about dose and preparations and serious interactions with tamoxifen.
options.why: Correct: this is NICE’s warning for people with a history of, or high risk of, breast cancer.

options.text: That it only interacts with anticoagulants, so there is no problem with tamoxifen.
options.why: NICE cites interactions with tamoxifen, anticoagulants and anticonvulsants.

items.explanation: For people with a history of, or high risk of, breast cancer, NICE explains that St John’s wort may relieve VMS, but there is uncertainty about dosage, persistence of effect and variation between preparations, and serious interactions, for example with tamoxifen, anticoagulants and anticonvulsants.

items.stem: A 53-year-old woman (fictional case) takes black cohosh for hot flashes and presents with dark urine and tiredness. Based on what NAMS 2023 reports, what is appropriate?

options.text: Continue it and add soy, because together they work better and do not affect the liver.
options.why: No source supports that combination, and NAMS recommends neither product.

options.text: Continue it, because the liver cases described are limited to doses far above the usual ones.
options.why: NAMS does not limit the cases to high doses; it reports the warning to stop it if liver symptoms appear.

options.text: Continue it, because NAMS recommends it at Level I and its benefit outweighs that risk.
options.why: NAMS does not recommend it (Level I, for insufficient evidence).

options.text: Stop it and assess liver function, given the reported cases of possible hepatotoxicity.
options.why: Correct: the USP warning reported by NAMS asks users to stop it and seek advice if liver symptoms appear.

items.explanation: NAMS 2023 reports cases of possible hepatotoxicity with black cohosh, and that a US Pharmacopeial Convention expert committee directed these products to carry a warning to stop them and seek advice if there is a liver disorder or liver symptoms appear. It also does not recommend it for VMS.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman (fictional case) with obesity and VMS asks which lifestyle change might help her hot flashes. According to NAMS 2023, which does it consider?

options.text: Weight loss, which NAMS considers for some women.
options.why: Correct: recommended at Levels II-III, with data from small studies.

options.text: Daily yoga, which NAMS recommends at Level I for VMS.
options.why: NAMS does not recommend yoga for VMS (Level II).

options.text: Intense aerobic exercise, more effective than hormone therapy.
options.why: NAMS does not recommend exercise for VMS, and in one study hormone therapy was far more effective.

options.text: Avoiding triggers and cooling down, recommended at Level I.
options.why: NAMS does not recommend cooling or avoiding triggers as treatment (Level II).

items.explanation: NAMS 2023 does not recommend cooling techniques, avoiding triggers, exercise or yoga (Level II), or dietary modification (Level III), as treatment for VMS. It does consider weight loss for some women (Levels II-III), with data from small non-randomised studies or post hoc analyses.

items.stem: According to NAMS 2023, which statement about acupuncture and stellate ganglion block for VMS is correct?

options.text: It recommends both at Level I as first-line alternatives to hormone therapy.
options.why: NAMS does not recommend acupuncture (Level II), and the block is Levels II-III, in selected women.

options.text: It recommends acupuncture (Level II) and does not recommend the block because it is invasive.
options.why: It is the other way round: it does not recommend acupuncture but does recommend the block in selected cases, weighing its risks.

options.text: It does not recommend acupuncture; the block might relieve moderate to very severe VMS in selected women.
options.why: Correct: acupuncture, Level II, not recommended; block, Levels II-III, recommended weighing its risks.

options.text: It recommends neither, because of a complete lack of trials in women with VMS.
options.why: NAMS does recommend stellate ganglion block in selected women (Levels II-III).

items.explanation: NAMS 2023 does not recommend acupuncture (Level II). It considers that stellate ganglion block might relieve moderate to very severe VMS in selected women, weighing the procedure’s risks (Levels II-III, recommended).

aemps-2026-mirena-ft.title: Fichas técnicas de Mirena 0,02 mg cada 24 horas y Levosert 0,02 mg cada 24 horas, sistemas de liberación intrauterinos (levonorgestrel 52 mg)
aemps-2026-mirena-ft.authors: AEMPS, CIMA; titulares Bayer Hispania y Gedeon Richter
aemps-2026-mirena-ft.population: Women using a 52 mg levonorgestrel IUD (Spain).
aemps-2026-mirena-ft.finding: Mirena: contraception (8 years) and idiopathic menorrhagia (5 years). Levosert: contraception and heavy menstrual bleeding. Neither includes endometrial protection during estrogen therapy.
aemps-2026-mirena-ft.limitations: Only Mirena sections 4.1 and 4.2 and Levosert section 4.1 were read (SmPCs dated 12 and 31 August 2026; nregistro 63158 and 80021); Levosert One was not read. Levosert SmPC: https://cima.aemps.es/cima/dochtml/ft/80021/FT_80021.html.

aemps-2026-progeffik-bijuva.title: Fichas técnicas de Progeffik 100 y 200 mg cápsulas blandas (progesterona) y Bijuva 1 mg/100 mg cápsulas blandas (estradiol/progesterona)
aemps-2026-progeffik-bijuva.population: Women with a uterus receiving estrogen; luteal insufficiency; luteal phase in assisted reproduction (Spain).
aemps-2026-progeffik-bijuva.finding: Oral Progeffik: adjunct to estrogen therapy in women with a uterus, among other indications; 200 mg/day for the last 2 weeks of each sequence. Vaginal route: luteal support in IVF and oocyte donation. Bijuva: continuous combined HRT in postmenopausal women with a uterus (≥ 12 months amenorrhoea).
aemps-2026-progeffik-bijuva.limitations: Progeffik sections 4.1 and 4.2 (SmPC dated 9 May 2019, old) and Bijuva 4.1 (SmPC dated 27 August 2026): https://cima.aemps.es/cima/dochtml/ft/85988/FT_85988.html.

aemps-2026-veoza-ft.title: Ficha técnica de Veoza 45 mg comprimidos recubiertos con película (fezolinetant)
aemps-2026-veoza-ft.authors: Agencia Española de Medicamentos y Productos Sanitarios (AEMPS), CIMA; titular Astellas Pharma Europe B.V.
aemps-2026-veoza-ft.population: Women with moderate to severe menopausal vasomotor symptoms (Spain/EU; centralised authorisation EMEA/H/C/005851).
aemps-2026-veoza-ft.finding: Indication: moderate to severe menopausal VMS; 45 mg once daily. Liver function tests before starting; do not start if ALT or AST ≥ 2 × ULN or total bilirubin is elevated; repeat monthly for the first 3 months and then as clinically indicated; stop if transaminases are ≥ 3 × ULN with bilirubin > 2 × ULN or symptoms, or > 5 × ULN.
aemps-2026-veoza-ft.limitations: Summary of product characteristics (not a guideline). Sections 4.1, 4.2 and 4.4 of the CIMA version were read (nregistro 1231771001; no revision date in the API). Medicine under additional monitoring.

fda-2026-veozah-label.title: VEOZAH (fezolinetant) tablets: prescribing information
fda-2026-veozah-label.authors: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), DailyMed/openFDA; Astellas Pharma US

nams-2022-hormone-therapy.title: The 2022 hormone therapy position statement of The North American Menopause Society
nams-2022-hormone-therapy.authors: The 2022 Hormone Therapy Position Statement Advisory Panel of The North American Menopause Society (now The Menopause Society); Faubion SS (lead), Crandall CJ, Davis L, El Khoudary SR, Hodis HN, Lobo RA, Maki PM, Manson JE, Pinkerton JV, Santoro NF, Shifren JL, Shufelt CL, Thurston RC, Wolfman W
nams-2022-hormone-therapy.population: Perimenopausal and postmenopausal women considering hormone therapy, in the United States context (FDA indications). Position statement by an expert panel of The North American Menopause Society, approved by its Board of Trustees; Menopause 2022;29(7):767-794. Updates the 2017 statement.
nams-2022-hormone-therapy.finding: Hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms and the genitourinary syndrome of menopause, and prevents bone loss and fracture. In women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset without contraindications, the benefit-risk ratio is favourable; when started after 60 or more than 10 years from menopause it appears less favourable because of greater absolute risks of coronary heart disease, stroke, venous thromboembolism and dementia. Women with a uterus need adequate progestogen. It does not need to be routinely stopped at 60–65. Compounded “bioidentical” hormones raise safety concerns, and saliva or urine testing to set the dose is unreliable.
nams-2022-hormone-therapy.limitations: Full PDF (28 pp.) read on the society's website. It is a consensus position statement, not a guideline with a formal systematic review: the “Key points” carry levels I (good and consistent evidence), II (limited or inconsistent) and III (consensus and expert opinion), with no separate strength grade. Much of the risk data comes from the WHI trials (oral conjugated equine estrogens and medroxyprogesterone acetate). US regulatory context. It was the current version as of 14-10-2026 (the society has published no later one).

nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy.title: The 2023 nonhormone therapy position statement of The North American Menopause Society
nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy.authors: The 2023 Nonhormone Therapy Position Statement Advisory Panel of The North American Menopause Society (now The Menopause Society); Shufelt CL (lead), Brown V, Carpenter JS, Chism LA, Faubion SS, Joffe H, Kling JM, Soares CN, Thurston RC
nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy.population: Women with menopausal vasomotor symptoms who are not good candidates for hormone therapy (contraindications such as estrogen-dependent cancers or cardiovascular disease) or prefer not to use it, including breast cancer survivors. Menopause 2023;30(6):573-590; updates the 2015 statement.
nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy.finding: Recommended: cognitive-behavioral therapy, clinical hypnosis, SSRIs/SNRIs, gabapentin and fezolinetant (Level I); oxybutynin (Levels I-II); weight loss and stellate ganglion block (Levels II-III). Not recommended: paced respiration (Level I); supplements and herbal remedies, including black cohosh (Levels I-III in table 2; I-II in the abstract); cooling techniques, avoiding triggers, exercise, yoga, mindfulness, relaxation, suvorexant, soy foods and extracts, equol, cannabinoids, acupuncture (Level II); clonidine (Levels I-III); dietary modification and pregabalin (Level III). Hormone therapy remains the most effective treatment.
nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy.limitations: Full PDF (18 pp.) read on the society's website; dosing table 1 (p. 6) and table 2 of recommendations with levels (p. 12). Consensus position statement with Levels I-III (no separate strength grade; each option is classified as “recommended” or “not recommended”). Many studies of non-drug options and supplements are small and use waitlist controls. It predates elinzanetant, still in development in 2023, and does not reflect any later labelling changes. It was the current version as of 14-10-2026.

nice-2026-ng23.title: Menopause: identification and management (NG23)
nice-2026-ng23.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2026-ng23.population: People in perimenopause and menopause in the UK health system; section 1.7 covers premature ovarian insufficiency in people under 40. Published November 2015, last updated 15 April 2026.
nice-2026-ng23.finding: From age 45, identify perimenopause (recently started vasomotor symptoms and cycle changes) and menopause (no period for 12 months without hormonal contraception) clinically, without laboratory tests; do not use AMH, inhibins, oestradiol, antral follicle count or ovarian volume [2015]. Offer HRT for vasomotor symptoms [2015]; consider menopause-specific CBT [2024]; fezolinetant when HRT is unsuitable (TA1143); do not routinely offer SSRIs, SNRIs or clonidine as first-line treatment for vasomotor symptoms alone [2015]. Combined HRT with a uterus and oestrogen-only HRT after total hysterectomy, at the lowest effective dosage [2024], reviewed at 3 months and then annually [2015]. VTE risk is not increased with transdermal HRT but is with oral HRT; consider transdermal HRT if VTE risk is increased, including a BMI over 30 kg/m² [2015]. Breast cancer risk rises with combined HRT according to duration, and very little or not at all with oestrogen-only HRT [2024]. POI (1.7, 2015 recommendations): diagnosis with symptoms, including infrequent or absent periods, and raised FSH on 2 samples 4–6 weeks apart; do not diagnose on a single blood test or use AMH routinely. Offer replacement with HRT or a combined hormonal contraceptive, until at least the age of natural menopause unless contraindicated; HRT may have a more beneficial effect on blood pressure than a combined oral contraceptive; both offer bone protection; HRT is not a contraceptive.
nice-2026-ng23.limitations: Full PDF (105 pp., 15-04-2026 version) read. The POI recommendations have not been updated since 2015 and predate the 2024 ESHRE guideline (which requires a single FSH). It gives no numerical FSH threshold. UK health-system context. For menopause at the usual age (aged 45 or over), NICE advises against offering HRT for primary or secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease (1.6.4) or for dementia prevention (1.6.5) [2024]; these do not apply to POI, where ESHRE does recommend HRT for those reasons.
